title: The new Welsh Liberal Democrats leader who survived two near-death experiences
excerpt: David Chadwick was left totally paralysed after developing a rare condition. Now he's the leader of the Liberal Democrats in Wales and says his traumatic experiences have left him desperate to help others
content:
New Welsh Lib Dem leader was left paralysed and survived two near-death experiences

David Chadwick was left totally paralysed after developing a rare condition. Now he's the leader of the Liberal Democrats in Wales and says his traumatic experiences have left him desperate to help others

13:45, 16 Nov 2026Updated 14:16, 16 Nov 2026

It is surviving not one, but two near-death experiences that were the motivation for David Chadwick entering politics.

‌

‌

Since 2024, he has been the MP for Brecon, Radnor and Cwm Tawe and the sole Liberal Democrat representative in Westminster from a Welsh constituency.

‌

When Jane Dodds resigned as Welsh leader, party rules meant he was the only eligible candidate to succeed her. There was no contest, and now, from today (November 16) he can add "leader of the Welsh Liberal Democrats" to his CV.

David Chadwick was selected in summer 2022 for the seat, having quit his job and moved to Brecon to campaign. Ahead of the general election, he did a year's full time campaigning, saying he spoke personally to some 3,000 people and driving 20,000 miles across the vast patch to do so.

The now 34-year-old grew up in Gloucester to a mum from Maesteg. His parents divorced when he was young and he has six younger siblings.

‌

The dad-of-two has a personal story of defying not one, but two near-death experiences and they are the reason he has entered politics.

Having been accepted into the British Army's intelligence corps at 19, he was injured and told to return in two years, so he went to The Hague in 2012 to study at Leiden University where he studied politics, economics, languages and history.

‌

On his way to a night out with friends, David was hit by a car which went through a red light. His father was called and told his son would be a "vegetable" when he woke up.

But David came around from his coma, waking up in a hospital bed wondering why he was there and seeing that his right leg had been broken.

‌

In 2014, he decided to go to study in Argentina but developed Guillain-Barré syndrome, which left him totally paralysed. His recovery took three years.

The incredibly rare auto-immune disease affects the nerves and kills 10% of those who contract it, while 70% make a full recovery. He admitted ahead of the election he wasn't entirely back to full strength.

‌

He moved back to the UK in 2018 because he wanted to become an MP and in 2019 stood in North Dorset before being elected in 2024.

Since being elected, he has used his own experiences to talk about healthcare and disabilities. He spoke in a debate about the UK Government's Access to Work scheme, citing his own experiences.

‌

"When I was paralysed with Guillain-Barré syndrome, I know first-hand how frightening it is to wonder if you will ever be able to work again," he said. "For many disabled people today, that fear is being made worse by a system that is supposed to support them."

‌

He further referenced that in his speech after being announced as leader. "10 years ago I couldn't have imagined that I would be standing here today. In fact, there was a time when I wasn't sure whether I would ever be able to stand again," he said.

"When I was 19, I was involved in a serious car accident while studying abroad. A few years later, aged 22, I developed a rare illness called Guillain-Barré syndrome, which left me completely paralysed.

‌

"I went from being a healthy, independent young man, travelling the world and planning my future, to being entirely dependent on others. It changed my life.

"It taught me how quickly any of us can find ourselves needing help, and how much our futures can depend on the care and support available to us.

‌

"It gave me a profound appreciation for the importance of protecting our NHS and public services and during my recovery, I made myself a promise: if I got better, I wanted to spend my life making a difference to others. That promise is one of the reasons I entered politics."

Asked why he wanted to be an MP in Wales, he said before the election: "Wales is such a big part of my identity and the part of the UK I know best.

‌

"Nobody wants to join the Liberal Democrats because you want to be Prime Minister, you join because you believe in what the party believes in. I know our time on this planet is fleeting and I want to use it to do some good.

"I've got six younger siblings, so I've always been taught to take responsibility for others and what I've seen in the last decade or 15 years is everything goes back to politics."
